Group Theory and Continuous Transformations

Purdue University

A collection of actions¶

Think of the things we can do to an object: rotate it, translate it, or exchange two identical parts. We can perform one action and then another. We can ask which action does nothing, and which action undoes a previous one.

Group theory studies this structure of combining actions. The elements need not be numbers or matrices; what matters is how they combine. This gives us a common language for rotations, permutations, and symmetries of molecules.

Let’s first define a group, then use rotations, integers, and permutations to see what the definition means.

Definition 1 (Group)

A group is a set GGG together with an operation, written ababab, satisfying:

  1. Closure: if a,b∈Ga,b\in Ga,b∈G, then ab∈Gab\in Gab∈G.

  2. Associativity: (ab)c=a(bc)(ab)c=a(bc)(ab)c=a(bc).

  3. Identity: there is an element eee such that ea=ae=aea=ae=aea=ae=a for every aaa.

  4. Inverses: each aaa has an element a−1a^{-1}a−1 such that aa−1=a−1a=eaa^{-1}=a^{-1}a=eaa−1=a−1a=e.

The letters a,ba,ba,b stand for arbitrary group elements, and eee denotes the identity. Depending on the group, eee may be 0 (addition), 1 (multiplication of numbers), or I\mathbf II (matrix multiplication).

The operation need not be ordinary multiplication. For transformations, it is composition: ababab means do bbb first, then aaa.

Associativity is not the same as commutativity. Associativity changes the parentheses without changing the order. If ab=baab=baab=ba for every pair, the group is called abelian, or commutative. Otherwise it is nonabelian.

Examples of groups¶

Four quarter-turns¶

Consider the set {1,i,−1,−i}\{1,i,-1,-i\}{1,i,−1,−i} under multiplication. These represent rotations through multiples of a quarter-turn. Their multiplication table is

×\times×1iii-1−i-i−i
11iii-1−i-i−i
iiiiii-1−i-i−i1
-1-1−i-i−i1iii
−i-i−i−i-i−i1iii-1

Every entry stays in the set. The identity is 1, and each element has an inverse; in particular, i−1=−ii^{-1}=-ii−1=−i. Associativity comes from complex multiplication.

All four elements are powers of iii, with i4=1i^4=1i4=1. This is the cyclic group C4C_4C4​. Here iii is called a generator because repeated multiplication produces the whole group. Later we will meet the related, but different, idea of an infinitesimal generator for continuous transformations.

Integers under addition¶

The integers form a group under addition. Adding two integers gives an integer; addition is associative; the identity is 0; and the inverse of nnn is −n-n−n. This group is abelian.

Permutations of three objects¶

Label three objects 1,2,31,2,31,2,3. Their six possible permutations form the group S3S_3S3​ under composition. Every permutation can be undone.

Let a=(12)a=(12)a=(12) exchange objects 1 and 2, and let b=(23)b=(23)b=(23) exchange objects 2 and 3. Track object 1:

ab: 1→b1→a2,ba: 1→a2→b3.ab:\ 1\xrightarrow{b}1\xrightarrow{a}2, \qquad ba:\ 1\xrightarrow{a}2\xrightarrow{b}3.ab: 1b​1a​2,ba: 1a​2b​3.
(1)

The results differ, so ab≠baab\ne baab=ba. This is a finite nonabelian group.

The symmetries of an equilateral triangle provide a geometric version: three rotations, including the identity, and three reflections permute its vertices. This group is isomorphic to S3S_3S3​—there is a one-to-one correspondence preserving composition. Molecular point groups use the same idea: retain only the spatial operations that leave a molecular configuration unchanged, allowing identical atoms to exchange places.

A non-example: nonnegative integers under addition¶

The set {0,1,2,3,…}\{0,1,2,3,\ldots\}{0,1,2,3,…} is closed under addition, addition is associative, and 0 is an identity. But 3 has no additive inverse in this set: we would need -3. Therefore this set is not a group under addition.

The set and the operation must both be specified. The integers under addition form a group, but the integers under multiplication do not: for example, 2 has no multiplicative inverse among the integers.

Continuous transformations and generators¶

Unlike the discrete quarter-turn group, a continuous rotation can be made arbitrarily small. To define a generator by a derivative, we consider a differentiable family of matrices. We focus first on a single real parameter; rotations about different axes will require different generators.

From a small change to a finite transformation¶

A rotation through a finite angle can be built from many small rotations. More generally, suppose T(t)\mathbf T(t)T(t) describes a continuous family of transformations satisfying the identity and composition laws

T(0)=I⏟identity law,T(t+s)=T(t)T(s)⏟composition law.\underbrace{\mathbf T(0)=\mathbf I}_{\text{identity law}}, \qquad \underbrace{\mathbf T(t+s)=\mathbf T(t)\mathbf T(s)}_{\text{composition law}}.identity lawT(0)=I​​,composition lawT(t+s)=T(t)T(s)​​.
(2)

Here t,s∈Rt,s\in\mathbb Rt,s∈R. In particular, T(t)T(−t)=T(0)=I\mathbf T(t)\mathbf T(-t)=\mathbf T(0)=\mathbf IT(t)T(−t)=T(0)=I, so each transformation has an inverse. This is called a one-parameter group of transformations. The parameter might be time or angle: adding parameters corresponds to composing transformations. We assume the family is smooth in this parameter. Near zero, write

T(δt)=I+δt G+O(δt2),G=dTdt∣t=0.\mathbf T(\delta t)=\mathbf I+\delta t\,\mathbf G+O(\delta t^2), \qquad \mathbf G=\left.\frac{d\mathbf T}{dt}\right|_{t=0}.T(δt)=I+δtG+O(δt2),G=dtdT​∣∣​t=0​.
(3)

The matrix G\mathbf GG is the generator: it specifies the first change away from the identity. To advance the transformation from ttt to t+δtt+\delta tt+δt, compose the transformation already accumulated, T(t)\mathbf T(t)T(t), with one additional infinitesimal step, T(δt)\mathbf T(\delta t)T(δt).

Theorem 1 (Differential equation generated by G\mathbf GG)

If T(t)\mathbf T(t)T(t) is a differentiable one-parameter group and

G=dTdt∣t=0,\mathbf G=\left.\frac{d\mathbf T}{dt}\right|_{t=0},G=dtdT​∣∣​t=0​,
(4)

then

dTdt=GT(t),T(0)=I.\boxed{\frac{d\mathbf T}{dt}=\mathbf G\mathbf T(t)}, \qquad \mathbf T(0)=\mathbf I.dtdT​=GT(t)​,T(0)=I.
(5)
Proof 1

The composition law gives

T(t+δt)=T(δt)T(t).\mathbf T(t+\delta t)=\mathbf T(\delta t)\mathbf T(t).T(t+δt)=T(δt)T(t).
(6)

Therefore

T(t+δt)−T(t)δt=T(δt)T(t)−IT(t)δt=[T(δt)−Iδt]T(t).\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathbf T(t+\delta t)-\mathbf T(t)}{\delta t} &=\frac{\mathbf T(\delta t)\mathbf T(t)-\mathbf I\mathbf T(t)}{\delta t}\\ &=\left[\frac{\mathbf T(\delta t)-\mathbf I}{\delta t}\right]\mathbf T(t). \end{aligned}δtT(t+δt)−T(t)​​=δtT(δt)T(t)−IT(t)​=[δtT(δt)−I​]T(t).​
(7)

Taking the limit δt→0\delta t\to0δt→0 gives

dTdt=dTdt∣t=0T(t)=GT(t).\frac{d\mathbf T}{dt} =\left.\frac{d\mathbf T}{dt}\right|_{t=0}\mathbf T(t) =\mathbf G\mathbf T(t).dtdT​=dtdT​∣∣​t=0​T(t)=GT(t).
(8)

Thus T(t)\mathbf T(t)T(t) describes the finite transformation accumulated so far, while G\mathbf GG gives its instantaneous rate of change. A single matrix G\mathbf GG therefore determines the whole family. We now solve the differential equation that relates them.

The matrix exponential as evolution¶

The previous section reduced the composition law to the initial-value problem

dTdt=GT(t),T(0)=I.\boxed{ \frac{d\mathbf T}{dt}=\mathbf G\mathbf T(t), \qquad \mathbf T(0)=\mathbf I.}dtdT​=GT(t),T(0)=I.​
(9)

For the scalar equation dx/dt=gxdx/dt=gxdx/dt=gx with x(0)=1x(0)=1x(0)=1, the solution is x(t)=etgx(t)=e^{tg}x(t)=etg. The matrix equation has the same form, so this suggests

T(t)=etG.\mathbf T(t)=e^{t\mathbf G}.T(t)=etG.
(10)

We can verify this directly using the power-series definition:

etG=I+tG+t2G22!+t3G33!+⋯ .e^{t\mathbf G} =\mathbf I+t\mathbf G+\frac{t^2\mathbf G^2}{2!} +\frac{t^3\mathbf G^3}{3!}+\cdots.etG=I+tG+2!t2G2​+3!t3G3​+⋯.
(11)

Differentiating term by term gives

ddtetG=GetG,e0G=I.\frac{d}{dt}e^{t\mathbf G}=\mathbf G e^{t\mathbf G}, \qquad e^{0\mathbf G}=\mathbf I.dtd​etG=GetG,e0G=I.
(12)

These are exactly the differential equation and initial condition derived above. Therefore

T(t)=etG.\boxed{\mathbf T(t)=e^{t\mathbf G}}.T(t)=etG​.
(13)

The same result can be understood as the limit of many small transformation steps:

etG=lim⁡N→∞(I+tNG)N.e^{t\mathbf G}=\lim_{N\to\infty} \left(\mathbf I+\frac{t}{N}\mathbf G\right)^N.etG=N→∞lim​(I+Nt​G)N.
(14)

The parameter times the generator must be dimensionless. For time evolution, G\mathbf GG has units of inverse time.

Planar rotations as a worked example¶

Example 1 (Rotation transformations)

Let us apply the construction to planar rotations. Their composition adds angles, so the angle plays the role of the parameter ttt. For the planar rotation matrix,

R[θ]=(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ),G=dRdθ∣0=(0−110).\mathbf R[\theta]= \begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf G=\left.\frac{d\mathbf R}{d\theta}\right|_0 =\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.R[θ]=(cosθsinθ​−sinθcosθ​),G=dθdR​∣∣​0​=(01​−10​).
(15)

Since G2=−I\mathbf G^2=-\mathbf IG2=−I, the even and odd powers of its exponential separate:

eθG=Icos⁡θ+Gsin⁡θ=R[θ].e^{\theta\mathbf G} =\mathbf I\cos\theta+\mathbf G\sin\theta =\mathbf R[\theta].eθG=Icosθ+Gsinθ=R[θ].
(16)

This is the matrix version of Euler’s formula. The generator plays the algebraic role of iii: applying it twice gives minus the identity.

SO(2), U(1), and representations¶

Unlike four quarter-turns, all planar rotations form a continuous family. The complex numbers of unit magnitude form

U(1)={eiθ:θ∈R}.\mathrm U(1)=\{e^{i\theta}:\theta\in\mathbb R\}.U(1)={eiθ:θ∈R}.
(17)

Angles differing by 2π2\pi2π describe the same element. Multiplication is closed and associative; the identity is 1; and the inverse of eiθe^{i\theta}eiθ is e−iθe^{-i\theta}e−iθ. This is an abelian group.

The real rotation matrices in the example obey

R[α]R[β]=R[α+β],R[0]=I,R[θ]−1=R[−θ].\mathbf R[\alpha]\mathbf R[\beta]=\mathbf R[\alpha+\beta], \qquad \mathbf R[0]=\mathbf I, \qquad \mathbf R[\theta]^{-1}=\mathbf R[-\theta].R[α]R[β]=R[α+β],R[0]=I,R[θ]−1=R[−θ].
(18)

The matrices are orthogonal and have determinant one. Their group is SO(2): special orthogonal matrices in two dimensions.

The correspondence eiθ↔R[θ]e^{i\theta}\leftrightarrow\mathbf R[\theta]eiθ↔R[θ] preserves multiplication and is one-to-one, so U(1) and SO(2) are isomorphic. They express the same group structure using different mathematical objects.

A matrix representation assigns matrices to group elements while preserving their multiplication:

D(ab)=D(a)D(b).D(ab)=D(a)D(b).D(ab)=D(a)D(b).
(19)

Different representations can act on different vector spaces. Not every representation is one-to-one.

Matrix groups¶

All real n×nn\times nn×n matrices under multiplication do not form a group, because singular matrices have no inverse. Restrict to invertible matrices and we obtain the general linear group GL(n,R)\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb R)GL(n,R).

Closure follows from

det⁡(AB)=det⁡(A)det⁡(B)≠0.\det(\mathbf A\mathbf B)=\det(\mathbf A)\det(\mathbf B)\ne0.det(AB)=det(A)det(B)=0.
(20)

The identity and inverses are included, and matrix multiplication is associative.

Orthogonal matrices form a smaller group, O(nnn). For two orthogonal matrices,

(AB)T(AB)=BTATAB=I.(\mathbf A\mathbf B)^T(\mathbf A\mathbf B) =\mathbf B^T\mathbf A^T\mathbf A\mathbf B=\mathbf I.(AB)T(AB)=BTATAB=I.
(21)

Requiring determinant +1 gives SO(nnn). Such a group contained in another group, with the same operation, is called a subgroup.

Reflections alone are not a group. The product of two reflections has determinant +1, so it is not another reflection. Also the identity is not a reflection. The full orthogonal group includes both orientation-preserving and orientation-reversing operations.

Unitary matrices similarly form U(nnn), and those with determinant one form SU(nnn). We can now ask what restrictions these length-preserving groups place on their generators.

Unitary transformations and Hermitian generators¶

What must the generator look like if every transformation U(t)\mathbf U(t)U(t) is unitary? For a small parameter step δt\delta tδt,

U(δt)=I+δt G+O(δt2),U†(δt)=I+δt G†+O(δt2).\mathbf U(\delta t) =\mathbf I+\delta t\,\mathbf G+O(\delta t^2), \qquad \mathbf U^\dagger(\delta t) =\mathbf I+\delta t\,\mathbf G^\dagger+O(\delta t^2).U(δt)=I+δtG+O(δt2),U†(δt)=I+δtG†+O(δt2).
(22)

Now impose the unitary condition U†U=I\mathbf U^\dagger\mathbf U=\mathbf IU†U=I:

U†(δt)U(δt)=(I+δt G†)(I+δt G)+O(δt2)=I+δt(G†+G)+O(δt2).\begin{aligned} \mathbf U^\dagger(\delta t)\mathbf U(\delta t) &=\left(\mathbf I+\delta t\,\mathbf G^\dagger\right) \left(\mathbf I+\delta t\,\mathbf G\right) +O(\delta t^2)\\ &=\mathbf I+\delta t\left(\mathbf G^\dagger+\mathbf G\right) +O(\delta t^2). \end{aligned}U†(δt)U(δt)​=(I+δtG†)(I+δtG)+O(δt2)=I+δt(G†+G)+O(δt2).​
(23)

This must equal I\mathbf II for arbitrarily small δt\delta tδt. Subtracting I\mathbf II, dividing by δt\delta tδt, and taking the limit δt→0\delta t\to0δt→0 gives

G†+G=0.\mathbf G^\dagger+\mathbf G=0.G†+G=0.
(24)

The derivative generator is anti-Hermitian. It is often more convenient to write it in terms of a Hermitian matrix J\mathbf JJ:

G=−iJ,J†=J,U(t)=e−itJ.\mathbf G=-i\mathbf J,\qquad \mathbf J^\dagger=\mathbf J,\qquad \mathbf U(t)=e^{-it\mathbf J}.G=−iJ,J†=J,U(t)=e−itJ.
(25)

We will use this minus-sign convention here. One can instead use e+itJe^{+it\mathbf J}e+itJ, but then the corresponding generator changes sign.

Theorem 2 (A Hermitian generator produces unitary transformations)

If J†=J\mathbf J^\dagger=\mathbf JJ†=J and ttt is real, then e−itJe^{-it\mathbf J}e−itJ is unitary.

Proof 2

Let

U=e−itJ=∑n=0∞(−itJ)nn!=I−itJ+(−it)22!J2+⋯ .\mathbf U=e^{-it\mathbf J} =\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-it\mathbf J)^n}{n!} =\mathbf I-it\mathbf J+\frac{(-it)^2}{2!}\mathbf J^2+\cdots.U=e−itJ=n=0∑∞​n!(−itJ)n​=I−itJ+2!(−it)2​J2+⋯.
(26)

Now take the dagger term by term. Because ttt is real, (−it)∗=it(-it)^*=it(−it)∗=it. Because J\mathbf JJ is Hermitian,

(Jn)†=(J†)n=Jn.(\mathbf J^n)^\dagger=(\mathbf J^\dagger)^n=\mathbf J^n.(Jn)†=(J†)n=Jn.
(27)

Therefore

U†=(∑n=0∞(−it)nJnn!)†=∑n=0∞((−it)n)∗(Jn)†n!=∑n=0∞(it)nJnn!=eitJ.\begin{aligned} \mathbf U^\dagger &=\left(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-it)^n\mathbf J^n}{n!}\right)^\dagger\\ &=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{\bigl((-it)^n\bigr)^*(\mathbf J^n)^\dagger}{n!}\\ &=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(it)^n\mathbf J^n}{n!}\\ &=e^{it\mathbf J}. \end{aligned}U†​=(n=0∑∞​n!(−it)nJn​)†=n=0∑∞​n!((−it)n)∗(Jn)†​=n=0∑∞​n!(it)nJn​=eitJ.​
(28)

The exponents itJit\mathbf JitJ and −itJ-it\mathbf J−itJ commute because both are multiples of the same matrix. We may therefore combine them:

U†U=eitJe−itJ=eitJ−itJ=e0=I.\begin{aligned} \mathbf U^\dagger\mathbf U &=e^{it\mathbf J}e^{-it\mathbf J}\\ &=e^{it\mathbf J-it\mathbf J}\\ &=e^{\mathbf 0}=\mathbf I. \end{aligned}U†U​=eitJe−itJ=eitJ−itJ=e0=I.​
(29)

Thus U\mathbf UU is unitary.

For the planar example, J=iG\mathbf J=i\mathbf GJ=iG is Hermitian and R[θ]=e−iθJ\mathbf R[\theta]=e^{-i\theta\mathbf J}R[θ]=e−iθJ is still real. Complex notation does not force the resulting transformation to be complex.

An eigenvector of J\mathbf JJ with eigenvalue jjj acquires the phase e−itje^{-itj}e−itj. The generator’s eigenvalues specify the rates at which the components change phase.

Commutators and order¶

Theorem 3 (Commuting generators give commuting transformations)

Let J1\mathbf J_1J1​ and J2\mathbf J_2J2​ be Hermitian matrices with J1J2=J2J1\mathbf J_1\mathbf J_2=\mathbf J_2\mathbf J_1J1​J2​=J2​J1​. Then, for any real s,ts,ts,t,

e−isJ1e−itJ2=e−itJ2e−isJ1=e−i(sJ1+tJ2).e^{-is\mathbf J_1}e^{-it\mathbf J_2} =e^{-it\mathbf J_2}e^{-is\mathbf J_1} =e^{-i(s\mathbf J_1+t\mathbf J_2)}.e−isJ1​e−itJ2​=e−itJ2​e−isJ1​=e−i(sJ1​+tJ2​).
(30)
Proof 3

Set A=−isJ1\mathbf A=-is\mathbf J_1A=−isJ1​ and B=−itJ2\mathbf B=-it\mathbf J_2B=−itJ2​. Since AB=BA\mathbf A\mathbf B=\mathbf B\mathbf AAB=BA, every power of A\mathbf AA commutes with every power of B\mathbf BB. Expanding the exponentials therefore lets us exchange their order term by term:

eAeB=∑m,n≥0AmBnm!n!=∑m,n≥0BnAmm!n!=eBeA.\begin{aligned} e^{\mathbf A}e^{\mathbf B} &=\sum_{m,n\geq0}\frac{\mathbf A^m\mathbf B^n}{m!n!}\\ &=\sum_{m,n\geq0}\frac{\mathbf B^n\mathbf A^m}{m!n!} =e^{\mathbf B}e^{\mathbf A}. \end{aligned}eAeB​=m,n≥0∑​m!n!AmBn​=m,n≥0∑​m!n!BnAm​=eBeA.​
(31)

The ordinary binomial expansion is also valid when A\mathbf AA and B\mathbf BB commute, so this same double sum equals eA+Be^{\mathbf A+\mathbf B}eA+B. Replacing A\mathbf AA and B\mathbf BB gives the claimed result.

So two commuting generators give transformations that can be applied in either order. We can also combine them into one exponential. What happens when we do not know whether the generators commute? The difference between the two possible matrix products is called their commutator:

[A,B]=AB−BA.[\mathbf A,\mathbf B]=\mathbf A\mathbf B-\mathbf B\mathbf A.[A,B]=AB−BA.
(32)

To test when two small transformations can be brought into a single exponent, compare eϵAeϵBe^{\epsilon\mathbf A}e^{\epsilon\mathbf B}eϵAeϵB with eϵ(A+B)e^{\epsilon(\mathbf A+\mathbf B)}eϵ(A+B). The parameter ϵ\epsilonϵ lets us find the first term where they differ.

Theorem 4 (When can we combine two matrix exponentials?)

For square matrices A\mathbf AA and B\mathbf BB of the same size,

eϵAeϵB=eϵ(A+B)for all sufficiently small real ϵe^{\epsilon\mathbf A}e^{\epsilon\mathbf B} =e^{\epsilon(\mathbf A+\mathbf B)} \quad\text{for all sufficiently small real }\epsiloneϵAeϵB=eϵ(A+B)for all sufficiently small real ϵ
(33)

if and only if [A,B]=0[\mathbf A,\mathbf B]=\mathbf0[A,B]=0.

Proof 4

Expand both sides through second order:

eϵAeϵB=I+ϵ(A+B)+ϵ22(A2+2AB+B2)+O(ϵ3),eϵ(A+B)=I+ϵ(A+B)+ϵ22(A2+AB+BA+B2)+O(ϵ3).\begin{aligned} e^{\epsilon\mathbf A}e^{\epsilon\mathbf B} &=\mathbf I+\epsilon(\mathbf A+\mathbf B) +\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}(\mathbf A^2+2\mathbf A\mathbf B+\mathbf B^2) +O(\epsilon^3),\\ e^{\epsilon(\mathbf A+\mathbf B)} &=\mathbf I+\epsilon(\mathbf A+\mathbf B) +\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}(\mathbf A^2+\mathbf A\mathbf B+\mathbf B\mathbf A+\mathbf B^2) +O(\epsilon^3). \end{aligned}eϵAeϵBeϵ(A+B)​=I+ϵ(A+B)+2ϵ2​(A2+2AB+B2)+O(ϵ3),=I+ϵ(A+B)+2ϵ2​(A2+AB+BA+B2)+O(ϵ3).​
(34)

Subtracting gives

eϵAeϵB−eϵ(A+B)=ϵ22[A,B]+O(ϵ3).e^{\epsilon\mathbf A}e^{\epsilon\mathbf B} -e^{\epsilon(\mathbf A+\mathbf B)} =\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}[\mathbf A,\mathbf B]+O(\epsilon^3).eϵAeϵB−eϵ(A+B)=2ϵ2​[A,B]+O(ϵ3).
(35)

If the exponentials are equal for all sufficiently small ϵ\epsilonϵ, divide by ϵ2\epsilon^2ϵ2 and take ϵ→0\epsilon\to0ϵ→0. The commutator must vanish. Conversely, if the matrices commute, their powers can be rearranged as in the previous proof, and the exponentials combine for every ϵ\epsilonϵ.

Equality at just one value of ϵ\epsilonϵ does not imply that the matrices commute. The theorem concerns the whole family near zero. The permutation example showed that changing the order of two actions can change the result; here the commutator captures that effect for small matrix transformations.

A useful way to isolate it is to perform a small sequence and then reverse the individual steps:

eϵAeϵBe−ϵAe−ϵB=I+ϵ2[A,B]+O(ϵ3).e^{\epsilon\mathbf A}e^{\epsilon\mathbf B} e^{-\epsilon\mathbf A}e^{-\epsilon\mathbf B} =\mathbf I+\epsilon^2[\mathbf A,\mathbf B]+O(\epsilon^3).eϵAeϵBe−ϵAe−ϵB=I+ϵ2[A,B]+O(ϵ3).
(36)

The rightmost factor acts first. If the generators commute, the sequence returns exactly to the starting point. Otherwise a second-order change remains.

Noether’s theorem: symmetry and conservation¶

Why do we have conservation laws at all? Energy, momentum, and angular momentum can look like three separate rules. In 1918, the mathematician Emmy Noether showed that they have a common origin. In her paper Invariant Variation Problems, written amid work on the mathematical foundations of general relativity, she connected continuous symmetries to conservation laws.

The idea is fundamental to how we describe the physical universe: when the action governing a system is unchanged by a continuous transformation, a corresponding quantity is conserved. If the laws are the same after shifting an experiment in space, the corresponding quantity is momentum. Rotational symmetry gives angular momentum; symmetry under a shift in time gives energy. A symmetry can be broken by the surroundings, so the associated conservation statement must be checked for the system being studied.

Unlike the discrete turns of an equilateral triangle, these transformations can be made arbitrarily small. We will not derive Noether’s general theorem from the classical action here. Instead, we can see its quantum counterpart using the generators we have just introduced: a generator of a continuous symmetry is conserved during the system’s evolution.

Theorem 5 (Continuous symmetry and conservation (quantum form))

Let H\mathbf HH be a time-independent Hamiltonian, and let the time-independent Hermitian operator Q\mathbf QQ generate a family of transformations

U(s)=e−isQ/ℏ.\mathbf U(s)=e^{-is\mathbf Q/\hbar}.U(s)=e−isQ/ℏ.
(37)

The product sQ/ℏs\mathbf Q/\hbarsQ/ℏ is dimensionless. For a rotation, sss is an angle and Q/ℏ\mathbf Q/\hbarQ/ℏ is the dimensionless Hermitian generator J\mathbf JJ used above.

If U(s)HU(s)†=H\mathbf U(s)\mathbf H\mathbf U(s)^\dagger=\mathbf HU(s)HU(s)†=H for every real sss, then ⟨Q⟩\langle\mathbf Q\rangle⟨Q⟩ is constant in time for any state evolving under H\mathbf HH.

Why does invariance give conservation? Differentiate the symmetry condition at s=0s=0s=0. Since U(0)=I\mathbf U(0)=\mathbf IU(0)=I, we get

dds(U(s)HU(s)†)∣s=0=iℏ[H,Q]=0.\left.\frac{d}{ds}\bigl(\mathbf U(s)\mathbf H\mathbf U(s)^\dagger\bigr)\right|_{s=0} =\frac{i}{\hbar}[\mathbf H,\mathbf Q]=\mathbf 0.dsd​(U(s)HU(s)†)∣∣​s=0​=ℏi​[H,Q]=0.
(38)

The generator therefore commutes with the Hamiltonian. The Schrödinger equation then gives

ddt⟨Q⟩=iℏ⟨[H,Q]⟩=0.\frac{d}{dt}\langle\mathbf Q\rangle =\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle[\mathbf H,\mathbf Q]\rangle=0.dtd​⟨Q⟩=ℏi​⟨[H,Q]⟩=0.
(39)

Question 3 below asks you to fill in both steps. For example, if the dynamics are unchanged by rotations about zzz, the conserved quantity is the zzz component of angular momentum. Symmetry about one axis does not by itself imply conservation of the other components.

Homework¶

Identifying groups¶

Question 1: Which of these are groups?

For each set and operation below, decide whether it forms a group. If it does, explain closure and associativity, identify the identity, and explain how to find an inverse for each element. If it does not, identify at least one axiom that fails and give a specific example of the failure.

  1. The odd integers {…,−3,−1,1,3,…}\{\ldots,-3,-1,1,3,\ldots\}{…,−3,−1,1,3,…} under addition.

  2. The even integers {…,−4,−2,0,2,4,…}\{\ldots,-4,-2,0,2,4,\ldots\}{…,−4,−2,0,2,4,…} under multiplication.

  3. All real 2×22\times22×2 matrices under matrix multiplication.

  4. All invertible real 2×22\times22×2 matrices under matrix multiplication.

Question 2: Permutations and symmetries of a triangle

Label the vertices of an equilateral triangle A,B,CA,B,CA,B,C in counterclockwise order. A symmetry is a rotation or reflection that leaves the triangle in the same position, though it may exchange the labeled vertices. The six possible permutations of the vertices are

e,(ABC),(ACB),(AB),(AC),(BC).e,\quad (ABC),\quad (ACB),\quad (AB),\quad (AC),\quad (BC).e,(ABC),(ACB),(AB),(AC),(BC).
(40)

Here eee leaves every vertex fixed, (ABC)(ABC)(ABC) sends A→BA\to BA→B, B→CB\to CB→C, and C→AC\to AC→A, and (AB)(AB)(AB) exchanges AAA and BBB while fixing CCC.

  1. For each of the six permutations listed above, write down where it sends AAA, BBB, and CCC.

  2. Match each permutation to a symmetry of the triangle. Which are rotations, and which are reflections? For each reflection, say which vertex stays fixed.

These are two descriptions of the same group structure. We say two groups are isomorphic if we can match their elements one-to-one in a way that preserves how they combine. Here, each triangle symmetry matches a permutation of its vertices, and performing two symmetries in order gives the same vertex permutation as composing their matching permutations in that order.

Generators and continuous transformations¶

Assume H\mathbf HH is Hermitian and time independent.

    ddt⟨Q⟩=iℏ⟨ψ∣[H,Q]∣ψ⟩.\frac{d}{dt}\langle\mathbf Q\rangle =\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle\psi|[\mathbf H,\mathbf Q]|\psi\rangle.dtd​⟨Q⟩=ℏi​⟨ψ∣[H,Q]∣ψ⟩.
